finalResponse:
To bridge the gap between a 14-week lead time and the competitor’s 6-week standard—without triggering another catastrophic quality failure—the company must abandon the brute-force approach of simply asking the floor to "work faster." The previous spike in warranty claims was a direct result of compressing execution time without redesigning the process. 

To resolve the inter-departmental feuding and win back the 33% of lost deals, leadership must implement the **"Velocity with Integrity" Framework**. This strategy shifts the manufacturing model from a traditional Make-to-Order (MTO) system to a hybrid Assemble-to-Order (ATO) system, integrates Quality Assurance (QA) directly into the production flow, and unites the siloed departments under shared metrics.

Here is the comprehensive operations improvement plan.

---

### Part 1: Diagnostic & Time-Loss Identification (The Value Stream Map)
In industrial equipment, "touch time" (the actual hours spent building the product) is rarely the cause of a 14-week lead time. The culprit is **queue time**—time products spend waiting for parts, waiting for inspectors, or waiting for a batch to be finished. 

To identify where time is lost, the company must execute a **Value Stream Map (VSM)**. Time traps will predictably be found in four areas:
1.  **Front-End Delays (Sales to Prod):** Unclear order specifications, missing information, or engineering delays before manufacturing even begins.
2.  **Supply Chain Lag:** Waiting on long-lead-time raw materials or specialized components.
3.  **Batching & Queues:** Moving products in large batches rather than single-piece flow, causing 9 units to sit idle while the 10th is worked on.
4.  **The "Quality Bottleneck":** Treating inspections as an end-of-line destination rather than an in-process activity.

### Part 2: Operational & Supply Chain Interventions (Compressing the Schedule)
To sustainably reach a 6-to-8 week lead time, the company must decouple raw material procurement and sub-assembly from the actual customer order.

*   **Shift to Assemble-to-Order (ATO):** Instead of starting from scratch when an order drops, identify the common base architectures of the equipment. Build and stock "vanilla" sub-assemblies (base frames, standard motors, wiring harnesses) to a 60% completion state based on Sales forecasts. When a customized order is placed, Production only needs to execute the final 40% of customization. This instantly shaves 4 to 6 weeks off the quoted lead time.
*   **Supplier Risk Mitigation:** For highly specialized, long-lead-time components that cannot be pre-assembled, negotiate Vendor-Managed Inventory (VMI) agreements. Guarantee suppliers a certain volume of purchases over 12 months in exchange for them holding 30 days of buffer stock locally. 
*   **Implement Single-Piece Flow:** Break down large production batches. Moving equipment through the facility one unit at a time reduces work-in-progress (WIP) inventory, clears floor space, and drastically accelerates the throughput of individual orders.

### Part 3: Protecting Quality Gates (Ensuring Integrity)
The previous warranty crisis occurred because QA was bypassed or rushed. Quality cannot be an afterthought; it must be built into the pacing of the factory.

*   **Concurrent / In-Line Inspections:** Currently, equipment likely sits in a queue waiting to enter a QA lab. Instead, move certified QA inspectors *onto the production floor*. As sub-assemblies are completed, QA inspects them in-station. If a defect is found, it is fixed immediately, rather than waiting until the entire machine is built, which requires costly and time-consuming teardowns.
*   **Quality at the Source (Poka-Yoke):** Empower operators. Give line workers automated go/no-go gauges, standardized digital checklists, and torque-controlled tools. The operators perform the first-level check; the certified QA inspectors perform the official validation. 
*   **The "Hard Stop" Mandate:** Leadership must establish a non-negotiable rule: No product moves to the next station without passing its stage-gate certification. If Sales complains about a delay due to a defect, leadership must publicly back Quality. Doing it right the first time is always faster than fixing a warranty claim in the field.

### Part 4: Cross-Functional Alignment (Ending the Feud)
Sales blames Production for being slow; Production blames Sales for bad forecasts and Quality for bottlenecking; Quality blames Production for sloppy work and Sales for rushing. This is a symptom of misaligned Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). The departments must be re-aligned through shared goals and structural changes.

*   **Establish a Value Stream Manager:** Appoint a single leader responsible for the *entire* lifecycle of the order—from the moment Sales signs the contract to the moment the equipment is delivered. Production, QA, and Order Entry all matrix-report to this leader to ensure flow.
*   **The Daily "Stand-Up" Triad Meeting:** Institute a 15-minute daily morning meeting with the heads of Sales, Production, and Quality. They review the visual board of all active orders. Sales flags incoming customized orders; Production highlights supply bottlenecks; Quality flags defect trends. This forces daily communication and prevents finger-pointing.
*   **Shared KPIs:** Restructure bonus structures so that all three departments are judged on a blended metric:
    *   *Sales* can no longer just throw incomplete orders over the wall. They are graded on "Clean Order Entry" (percentage of orders submitted with 100% accurate engineering specs).
    *   *Production* is no longer graded solely on machine utilization. They are graded on "First-Pass Yield" (doing it right the first time without QA kicking it back).
    *   *Quality* is no longer graded just on defects caught. They are graded on "Inspection Turnaround Time" (how quickly they can certify and release a compliant product).

### Summary
By transitioning to an Assemble-to-Order model, the company can artificially compress lead times by doing 60% of the work before the customer even places the order. By embedding QA inspectors directly into the production line, the 14-week lead time can be systematically reduced to match the competitor’s 6 weeks without risking the catastrophic warranty failures of the past. Finally, aligning Sales, Production, and Quality under shared KPIs transforms them from warring factions into a unified engine focused on speed, accuracy, and market capture.

run.userPrompt:

The product requires certified quality inspections at multiple stages, and the last attempt to compress the schedule caused a spike in warranty claims that took two years to live down. Production, quality, and sales each blame the others' processes.

Develop an operations improvement plan that substantially reduces quoted lead time without compromising certified quality standards. Identify where time is actually lost, which process, inventory, scheduling, or supplier changes to make, how to protect quality gates, and how to align the three feuding functions around the plan.
